title: From Amritsar's Bylanes to the TIME100: Vikas Khanna's Unstoppable Rise as India's Global Culinary Ambassador
excerpt: The chef, filmmaker, and humanitarian becomes the first Indian culinary figure on TIME's list of the world's 100 most influential people, capping a year that also brought him Harvard's Person of the Year honour.
body:
Every Indian who has ever packed a tiffin of rajma-chawal for a long journey knows the quiet power of food as identity. For Vikas Khanna, the chef from Amritsar who once worked roofless kitchens and slept in a New York homeless shelter, that power has now been validated at the highest possible level: TIME magazine has named him to its 2026 TIME100 list of the world's most influential people.

## A Historic First for Indian Cuisine

Khanna's inclusion is a landmark moment — not just for one chef, but for an entire culinary tradition that has long been underrepresented on global prestige lists. While Indian software engineers, CEOs, and politicians have appeared on TIME100 before, Khanna is the first figure recognised primarily for his contribution to Indian food culture.

"Being on the 2026 TIME100 list is a matter of immense pride for me," Khanna said in a statement. "I owe this recognition to my grandmother, mother, and sister — they always believed in me. This achievement is a victory for India and our culinary legacy."

The honour follows close on the heels of another accolade: Harvard University's South Asian Association named Khanna its Person of the Year in April 2026, celebrating his role in showcasing India's rich culinary heritage on the international stage.

## From Junoon to Bungalow: Building an Empire

Khanna's journey reads like a Bollywood script stripped of melodrama and filled instead with grit. Born in Amritsar, he trained in India before moving to New York, where his Michelin-starred restaurant Junoon became a beacon of refined Indian dining for years. His latest venture, Bungalow in New York City, has taken the city by storm as what he calls "a vibrant cultural tribute to India's rich heritage and flavours through immersive dining experiences."

Beyond restaurants, Khanna has authored over 41 books documenting Indian culinary traditions, directed the acclaimed film *The Last Color*, and is preparing to release *Imaginary Rain*, a new culinary drama set in New York.

## Feeding India: The Humanitarian Chef

But perhaps his most consequential work has been outside the kitchen. Through his Feed India initiative during the COVID-19 pandemic, Khanna organised the distribution of meals to more than 30 million people across 135 cities — one of the largest such efforts by an individual anywhere in the world.

He also runs the South Asian Kid's Infinite Vision foundation, channelling his influence into systemic change for underprivileged communities.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For the estimated 4.4 million Indian Americans, Khanna's TIME100 moment is deeply personal. In a country where Indian food has long been reduced to "curry" in the popular imagination, his elevation signals a fundamental shift in how the world sees Indian culinary identity.

"What a milestone for Indian cuisine," Khanna said at the Harvard ceremony. "From the bylanes of Amritsar to the stage at Harvard University. This recognition is not just an award — it's a promise."

## What's Next

Khanna's influence shows no signs of slowing. With *Imaginary Rain* set for release later this year and Bungalow continuing to redefine Indian fine dining in New York, the chef from Amritsar is proving that Indian food's moment on the global stage is not a trend — it's a permanent arrival.

As he put it: "Every single morning at my restaurant, Bungalow, is a tribute to India."

*Sources: TIME Magazine, The Indian Eye, Indian Television, Curly Tales*
